title: Microsoft Service Outage Gives Software Giant Black Eye - Investor's Business Daily
content:
BREAKING: Nasdaq Has Best Week In Two Months, But Ends Below Key Level Microsoft (MSFT) stock wobbled Friday after a widespread outage of Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook and Teams, hobbled business and government users starting midday Thursday Eastern time. By Friday afternoon, Microsoft claimed to have had the situation mostly under control. It attributed the outage to cloud server issues. Microsoft stock ended the regular session Friday up a fraction to 523.88. In morning trades on the stock market today, Microsoft fell as much as 1.8% to 513.82, before recovering. The service outage was one of the company's most prolonged disruptions. Microsoft said it had no evidence of malicious activity. The Microsoft service outage impacted users in 74 countries and generated more than 130,000 reports on Downdetector, GlobalData reported Friday. The disruption left many users without email access. Evercore ISI analyst Kirk Materne estimated that the service outage impacted about 100 million paid seats of Microsoft 365. The company could be facing claims for service credits totaling $100 million to $400 million, he said. "This is obviously just a rough estimate, but the point is that against a $90 billion+ quarter, the impact from a monetary standpoint should be relatively benign," Materne said in a client note. "That said, it was obviously a major distraction for businesses and not a great look heading into (the company's) Ignite (conference) next week." In a post on X at 10:39 a.m. Eastern time Friday, Microsoft said the company was making "encouraging recovery progress." "We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us," Microsoft said. "We will continue to share more information as we have it, and for now we can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity. Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward." In a follow-up post at 1:05 p.m. Eastern time, Microsoft apologized for the disruption. "We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services," the company said. "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions." In a later post at 3:05 p.m. Eastern, Microsoft said its infrastructure was stabilizing, but it had work to do. "We do not have an ETA for full recovery yet," it said. Microsoft (MSFT) said on Friday afternoon that the outage, which prevented users from accessing its software tools, including email, was a technical issue unrelated to AI agents or "cyber". The company said it is seeing broad recovery and continues to restore service to the remaining customers and affected regions. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," said the company in a statement. "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents," added the company. Microsoft said the incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. The connectivity issues, which began Thursday, were being worked on for hours, with the company at one point indicating that servers that had been brought back online became unresponsive again. By Friday morning, Microsoft said it was seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific. "Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation continues across remaining affected infrastructure," said the update on X. On Thursday afternoon, Microsoft said users of Exchange Online, which powers Outlook email, as well as the company's Teams videoconferencing app and Copilot AI chatbot, may experience disruptions. In a separate post on X, the company said users "in any region" could be affected. Microsoft said it was rerouting connection traffic across its global infrastructure and restarting affected servers. Around 7:05 p.m. ET, Microsoft said some servers were becoming unresponsive again as traffic returned, underscoring that the company had not yet fully stabilized the outage. Friday morning, Microsoft said, "Our focus remains on stabilizing recovered infrastructure, completing mitigation in remaining impacted areas, and reducing delayed email queues and backlogs while we validate service consistency across connection methods." Microsoft (MSFT) said on Friday afternoon that the outage, which prevented users from accessing its software tools, including email, was a technical issue unrelated to AI agents or "cyber". The company said it is seeing broad recovery and continues to restore service to the remaining customers and affected regions. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," said the company in a statement. "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents," added the company. Microsoft said the incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. The connectivity issues, which began Thursday, were being worked on for hours, with the company at one point indicating that servers that had been brought back online became unresponsive again. By Friday morning, Microsoft said it was seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific. "Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation continues across remaining affected infrastructure," said the update on X. On Thursday afternoon, Microsoft said users of Exchange Online, which powers Outlook email, as well as the company's Teams videoconferencing app and Copilot AI chatbot, may experience disruptions. In a separate post on X, the company said users "in any region" could be affected. Microsoft said it was rerouting connection traffic across its global infrastructure and restarting affected servers. Around 7:05 p.m. ET, Microsoft said some servers were becoming unresponsive again as traffic returned, underscoring that the company had not yet fully stabilized the outage. Friday morning, Microsoft said, "Our focus remains on stabilizing recovered infrastructure, completing mitigation in remaining impacted areas, and reducing delayed email queues and backlogs while we validate service consistency across connection methods." While the disruption to Outlook, Teams and Copilot has put cloud reliability under scrutiny, the company’s aggressive AI infrastructure spending is creating a separate challenge for investors. Microsoft is growing rapidly, but sustaining that momentum requires enormous capital commitments. With MSFT approaching a key technical resistance zone, investors have more than one risk to assess. Microsoft’s latest global outage has exposed the risks of its growing dependence on cloud-based workplace services. The disruption, which began on November 12, affected Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot across multiple regions. BREAKING: Microsoft's Outlook, Teams and Copilot have been down for over 15 hours.Microsoft says it's not a cyberattack, but servers going down unexpectedly.$MSFT is down -3% in premarket. pic.twitter.com/o4xpAG8e2F The incident lasted more than 12 hours, disrupting businesses, government agencies and other organizations. Microsoft attributed the problem to server and infrastructure issues and said it had found no indication of malicious activity. Its recovery efforts initially struggled as some restored servers became unresponsive under returning traffic. The disruption also follows another Microsoft 365 service incident earlier this year, bringing reliability concerns back into focus. For enterprise customers, consistent uptime is central to Microsoft’s competitive position. Repeated failures could encourage large organizations to reconsider their dependence on a single cloud ecosystem. The immediate financial damage remains unclear, but the reputational risk is harder to measure. Investors will be watching Microsoft’s post-incident explanation and whether the company can demonstrate that its infrastructure is becoming more resilient. The second concern is the scale of Microsoft’s AI investment. The company is expanding data-center capacity to support Azure, AI workloads and growing demand for computing infrastructure. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditure for fiscal Q1 2027, while management expects calendar-year 2026 spending to reach approximately $170 billion. It also indicated that quarterly capital expenditure could exceed $50 billion in the December quarter. The investment is supported by strong demand. Azure revenue increased 48% in the September quarter, while Microsoft Cloud revenue rose 30% to $63.9 billion. Commercial remaining performance obligations also climbed 73% to $677 billion. However, the central question is how quickly that demand translates into returns. Heavy infrastructure spending can pressure free cash flow and operating margins, particularly when new capacity takes time to become productive. Microsoft’s own filings warn that slower AI adoption, underutilized infrastructure and rising computing costs could affect future returns. The company is therefore facing a demanding balance: invest enough to capture AI growth without allowing capital costs to outrun revenue generation. Microsoft’s cloud business remains a major strength, but sustaining its current growth rate will not be straightforward. Azure grew 48% in the latest quarter, and management expects growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency for the December quarter. However, Microsoft also acknowledged that customer demand continues to exceed available supply, while some third-party GPU capacity deliveries have been delayed. Microsoft stock price closed at $539.44 on November 13, gaining 1.08%. The stock is approaching a major supply zone between $550 and $560, where previous advances have encountered selling pressure. A sustained breakout above this region could strengthen the recovery and bring $575 into focus. On the downside, $515 is the immediate support area, followed by $490–$500. The broader demand zone sits around $375–$390, although that remains well below the current trading range. The moving averages continue to provide support beneath the current price, but the recent rejection near the supply zone suggests buyers have yet to establish control. A breakout above $560 would improve the technical outlook, while a decline below $515 could weaken the recovery. Microsoft’s long-term growth story remains supported by Azure expansion, enterprise software and AI demand. However, the latest outage has highlighted operational risks, while the company’s infrastructure spending raises questions about capital efficiency and future profitability. The next phase will depend on whether Microsoft can restore customer confidence, convert AI demand into sustainable revenue and maintain cloud growth without sacrificing margins. Microsoft tracks the incident as EX1550543 for Exchange Online and MO1550821 for the wider suite, per SecurityWeek. Japan’s government IT infrastructure was affected, Singapore’s Government Technology Agency lost email, and the Philippine Supreme Court said its operations were affected, the Associated Press reported. EV maker Workhorse postponed its earnings call, and IndiGo and Air India rerouted customer email. Microsoft said the strain came from “a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable,” with “a core process on affected servers” overwhelmed and “causing capacity loss,” according to Outlook India. At 01:48 GMT it narrowed that to the process “responsible for establishing secure connections,” ABC7 reported. A recent network configuration change coincided with the start, and Microsoft was reversing it to test whether it contributed. Microsoft reported partial recovery at 04:36 GMT but said it had “not been sustained.” A later post said its fixes were “not taking as expected,” per AP. Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president for Copilot, Agents and Platform, wrote that “there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.” Microsoft has promised a post-incident report once service is restored. Anthropic’s status page flagged elevated errors on its Microsoft 365 connector at 17:52 UTC Thursday. By 22:23 UTC it said the fault “is caused by a Microsoft 365 service incident,” with mail, calendar and search tools failing for most requests and Claude for Outlook also affected. OpenAI reported similar trouble connecting to Microsoft 365 tools, AP said. Microsoft’s own Copilot Chat and Copilot access to work data were also hit. Microsoft said the outage affected Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with Exchange Online, per AP, and that mailbox layer is what both Copilot and the third-party connectors read from. Coverage split on how MSFT stock traded Thursday, and the tape explains why. Shares stood at $528.53 just after 1 p.m. ET, then slid to $520.87 by 3:15 p.m., a 1.45% drop, according to intraday data from Fiscal.ai. They recovered to close at $523.00, up 0.36%, on 18.6 million shares against a 10-day average of 33.1 million. Friday’s pre-market drop in MSFT stock came as Nasdaq-100 futures slipped just 0.03% at 10:57 GMT, a day after Nvidia said Jensen Huang had resigned as chief executive, while Alphabet, whose Google Workspace competes with Microsoft 365, rose 0.98% pre-market. A $14.49 drop across 7.43 billion shares equals about $107.6 billion of market value. Nasdaq-100 futures were flat while MSFT stock fell 2.77% pre-market, so the $107.6 billion markdown is a Microsoft-specific outage discount. The pre-market print sits below the $520.19 year-end bear case in FinanceFeeds’ 24 October Microsoft stock prediction. Below that, $504.96 was the 2 November intraday low, close to the $505 reference. At the pre-market price, MSFT stock is down 9.06% from its $559.15 high on 4 November. Shareholders of record on 19 November receive the $0.98 quarterly dividend, payable 10 December, under Microsoft’s 15 September declaration. The ex-dividend date is also 19 November, per Yahoo Finance. The fundamentals under MSFT stock were set before the outage, with Microsoft Cloud revenue up 30% to $63.9 billion in the September quarter and Azure up 48%. Microsoft spent $41 billion on capex in the June quarter, and the post-incident report will show whether a configuration change undid that capacity for a day. The next earnings report is expected around 27 January. title: What caused the Microsoft outage? Update issued with Outlook and Teams down - Yahoo Finance UK
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Microsoft has been hit by a huge outage, taking down Outlook and Teams – causing chaos across the world. The issues began on Thursday afternoon and have continued into Friday. Because so many organisations rely on Microsoft's tools, it has already caused problems everywhere from hospitals to airports. Microsoft said the problems were affecting its 365 Services, which include the messaging app Teams, email service Outlook and its Copilot AI tool. More than 430 million people use those services, according to Microsoft's website, including many of the world's biggest companies and most important organisations. Amid the disruption, many speculated that the problems could be the result of a cyber attack. That gained particular prominence because of widespread fears that the growing power of artificial intelligence tools could bring disruptive outages of this kind. But experts and Microsoft itself both say that there is no evidence the technical issues are the result of a cyber attack. Instead, it seems to be a more innocent, if equally concerning, mistake. Microsoft said the outage came because of "elevated load", not because of an increased amount of traffic but because its servers had become "unexpectedly unavailable". It has not said exactly why those servers became unavailable – previous similar problems have been caused by everything from physical incidents such as fires at data centres to errant updates that take the systems online, which appears most likely in this case. The company said it had no evidence of "malicious activity" and executive vice president Charles Lamanna said Microsoft had ruled out a cyber attack. Experts agreed that it appeared to be the result of a "bug" – though the exact details of it remain unclear. "Rather than a cyber attack, most likely this was caused by an update to software which contained a bug," said Tom Worthington, from the Australian National University. "It is unlikely there will be a loss of data, just inconvenience as systems are manually rolled back to the last good copy of the software. This is a useful reminder not to be dependent on one mobile phone company or email service." Despite the fact that there was no evidence of a hack, security experts warned that it could nonetheless be used by cyber criminals to launch attacks of their own. "Although the Microsoft outage is not a cybersecurity issue, bad actors will be looking to take advantage of concerned individuals, offering a resolution or assurances," said Aiden Sinnott, principal threat researcher at Sophos Counter Threat Unit. "At this time, even more so than usual, people should exercise caution when receiving emails, texts or calls purporting to be from Microsoft or other affected businesses, particularly banks or shops. Be aware of requests for urgent action, sharing of personal information, and avoid clicking on links sent via message or email." Experts also warned that it was yet another reminder that organisations need to work harder on both resilience, to ensure that issues of this nature are less likely, and redundancy to ensure that they could continue even when they do happen. "With so much of the world's tech landscape reliant on a handful of giants, when one fails it can quickly evolve into a global IT blackout. Services from email to AI virtual assistants connected to Microsoft can stall for users, grinding many organisations to a halt," said Jake Moore, global cybersecurity adviser at ESET. "This kind of outage is exactly why services haven't become fully digital. For now, affected users who need to contact someone should rely on alternate forms of communication like phone calls. For big tech firms, this is yet another lesson on the importance of cyber resilience and having fallback plans in place for when critical servers fail." title: MSFT Dips 3% as Microsoft Scrambles to Resolve Historic Outlook Outage - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft (MSFT) shares edged down 3% in extended trading following Thursday’s session, as a massive global outage across Outlook and Microsoft 365 stretched past 12 hours into Friday. Investors have treated the incident largely as a temporary operational hiccup rather than a fundamental threat to Microsoft’s cloud business. The stock was already pulled back 6% from its early-November record high ($555) amid broader tech volatility and scrutiny over AI infrastructure spending. Scope & Impact: Beginning Thursday afternoon (Nov. 12), the disruption centered on Exchange Online—the backend infrastructure powering Outlook—and spilled over into Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, OneDrive, and Copilot 365. Downdetector logged roughly 200,000 user issue reports across Microsoft services, peaking at over 130,000 for Outlook alone. The prolonged blackout forced financial trading desks and exchanges (including Euronext) to revert to phone and fax communications, while disrupting airlines, schools, healthcare networks (such as the UK’s NHS), and government agencies across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. Microsoft stated there is no indication of a cyberattack. After initial remediation attempts failed to take hold, Microsoft deployed a targeted patch to a connection-routing component early Friday, reporting “positive results for server stability” as it works to restart affected infrastructure and fully restore services.

Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) enters November 13, 2026, facing renewed scrutiny over its cloud infrastructure, artificial intelligence investment strategy and growing competition in enterprise productivity software. Microsoft shares closed November 12 at $523, valuing the company at approximately $3.88 tn. The stock has retreated nearly 6% from its November 4 record closing price of $555.80, reflecting broader concerns about AI valuations and the profitability of expanding computing infrastructure. According to a survey of 58 Wall Street analysts, Microsoft’s average 12-month stock price target stands at $636.12, implying potential upside of 21.6%. The median forecast is $631, while individual estimates range from $440 to $870. The consensus remains strongly positive, with 53 analysts recommending Buy or Strong Buy, five assigning Hold ratings and none recommending Sell. A separate compilation covering 51 analysts produces a lower average target of $609.54, reflecting differences in coverage and methodology. StockAnalysis.com+1 Recent investment bank forecasts suggest that confidence in Microsoft’s cloud and AI businesses remains intact. However, the emphasis has shifted from measuring demand for AI services to assessing infrastructure utilization, capital efficiency and the sustainability of earnings growth. Several major investment banks revised their Microsoft forecasts upward following the company’s October earnings report, although their valuations reflect different expectations for AI monetization. Wells Fargo raised its price target from $725 to $750 while maintaining an Overweight rating. Bernstein increased its forecast from $662 to $722 and retained an Outperform recommendation. UBS established a $700 target following the quarterly results. Citi maintained a Buy rating and a $680 target in its November 12 update, focusing on Microsoft’s opportunities in enterprise AI agents, Copilot adoption and the infrastructure needed to manage autonomous workflows. Morgan Stanley, Piper Sandler, Stifel and Jefferies have maintained forecasts around $650. RBC Capital Markets has a $640 target, while Evercore ISI expects $635. These estimates represent a relatively narrow group of bullish valuations compared with the wider range of Wall Street forecasts. More conservative projections include Barclays at $610 and Guggenheim at $595. Both remain positive on the shares but assign less upside than the most optimistic investment banks. Benzinga+2 The differences increasingly concern Microsoft’s ability to convert AI-related spending into profitable revenue. Bullish forecasts place greater weight on Azure growth, enterprise AI adoption and Microsoft’s distribution advantage. More cautious valuations leave less room for further multiple expansion until higher infrastructure spending produces stronger cash returns. Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 bn for its fiscal first quarter of 2027, ended September 30, representing 19% year-over-year growth. Operating income rose 21% to $45.9 bn, while adjusted earnings per share increased 18% to $4.89. The results exceeded Wall Street expectations for both revenue and profitability. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 bn, increasing 30%, while Azure revenue surged 48%. Management attributed the cloud performance to growing demand for AI infrastructure, higher consumption of Microsoft Foundry services and improved utilization of existing computing capacity. The company expects Azure revenue growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency during its fiscal second quarter, despite delays in the delivery of third-party GPU capacity. Microsoft’s commercial remaining performance obligations increased 73% to $677 bn. Approximately 30% of those contracted obligations are expected to convert into revenue over the following 12 months. However, commercial bookings declined 12%, primarily because the year-earlier period included substantial Azure commitments. The difference between bookings and remaining performance obligations illustrates how large cloud contracts can create significant quarterly volatility without necessarily indicating a corresponding change in underlying demand. Microsoft+1 The accelerating cloud business provides substantial support for Microsoft’s earnings outlook. The principal uncertainty concerns profitability as an increasing share of revenue comes from computing-intensive AI workloads. Microsoft’s infrastructure investment program has become one of the central considerations in institutional valuation models. Capital expenditures reached $45.2 bn during the September quarter, with approximately three-quarters allocated to shorter-lived assets, primarily CPUs and GPUs, alongside related memory and storage equipment. Operating cash flow increased 29% to $58 bn, but free cash flow was $18.6 bn after infrastructure investment. Management expects capital expenditures to exceed $50 bn in the December quarter. Its latest guidance places calendar 2026 spending at approximately $170 bn, following delays in third-party capacity deliveries. That updated outlook is below the $175 bn to $190 bn range referenced in some secondary forecasts. Microsoft expects capital investment to accelerate again during the second half of fiscal 2027 as delayed computing capacity becomes available and additional processors are deployed. The company also reported Microsoft Cloud gross margins of 66%, reflecting a greater revenue contribution from Azure. Management expects the figure to decline to approximately 65% in the December quarter as the business mix continues to shift toward cloud infrastructure. This creates a valuation challenge. Faster Azure revenue growth can support higher earnings estimates, but additional depreciation, equipment replacement and financing costs may limit the improvement in cash generation. Current analyst estimates imply approximately $396 bn in revenue for fiscal 2027, representing growth of about 19% from fiscal 2026. Adjusted earnings are projected at around $20.01 per share, placing Microsoft’s forward earnings multiple near 26 times its latest closing price. The valuation assumes that Microsoft can maintain substantial revenue expansion while absorbing the cost of its AI infrastructure program. A slowdown in Azure growth or weaker infrastructure profitability would make that multiple more difficult to sustain. Microsoft+2 Microsoft’s latest global service disruption has introduced another risk into the stock outlook. The outage began on November 12 and continued into Asian business hours on November 13, affecting Outlook, Microsoft Teams, Exchange Online, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services. Downdetector recorded nearly 130,000 reports of Outlook problems in the United States at the peak of the disruption, with incidents reported across 74 countries and territories. The incident affected government organizations in Australia, Japan and the United States, including the U.S. House of Representatives and Australian security agencies. Indian airlines experienced interruptions to email support services, while financial institutions in Taiwan reported operational problems, including a disrupted bond repurchase transaction. OpenAI and Anthropic also experienced problems with Microsoft 365 connectors, demonstrating how failures in Microsoft’s infrastructure can affect AI services operated by other companies. Microsoft identified overloaded server processes, unexpected server failures and traffic-routing problems as contributing factors. Some restarted servers became unresponsive again when user traffic returned. By early November 13, the company reported improvements in server stability following configuration patches and traffic optimization measures, but a complete restoration had not been confirmed. Microsoft said it had found no evidence of malicious activity and planned to release a detailed post-incident report after resolving the disruption. The incident follows a Microsoft 365 outage in January 2026 and previous Azure-related disruptions, adding to questions about the resilience of increasingly interconnected enterprise systems. CIO+2 The immediate financial effect remains difficult to quantify. No verified estimate of lost revenue, customer compensation or additional operating expenses has been disclosed. Microsoft’s subscription-based business model also limits the probability of an immediate customer exodus. Large organizations face substantial switching costs because Microsoft 365 integrates email, documents, identity management, security and collaboration software. Nevertheless, repeated disruptions could influence contract renewals, enterprise procurement decisions and the willingness of customers to concentrate additional AI workloads with a single cloud provider. For investors, the longer-term risk is not necessarily the cost of one outage but whether reliability concerns weaken Microsoft’s pricing power or slow enterprise cloud adoption. Microsoft also faces increasing competition from AI developers moving beyond conversational assistants into productivity applications. On November 10, Anthropic introduced Claude Sheets and Claude Whiteboards in beta, alongside the broader availability of its interactive dashboard product, Claude Data. Claude Sheets allows users to create spreadsheets with formulas, formatting and multiple tabs through natural-language instructions. Whiteboards supports collaborative planning, while Claude Data provides interactive analysis and visualization. Anthropic also previewed Claude Meetings, an AI assistant designed to participate in meetings and automate follow-up tasks. The expansion introduces direct competition for Microsoft Excel and parts of the wider Microsoft 365 ecosystem. Microsoft 365 commercial and consumer products generated approximately $111 bn in fiscal 2026 revenue, equivalent to roughly one-third of Microsoft’s total annual sales. Under Microsoft’s previous reporting structure, Productivity and Business Processes generated $83.9 bn in operating income, accounting for approximately 54% of total company operating profit. That segment also included LinkedIn and Dynamics, so the figure should not be interpreted as Microsoft 365 operating profit alone. The commercial significance of Anthropic’s products remains uncertain. Claude Sheets currently offers simpler spreadsheet functionality than Excel and supports exporting files into Microsoft’s established formats. Enterprise deployment is also cautious. Anthropic enabled its new applications by default for Team plans but not for Enterprise customers. Microsoft retains substantial distribution advantages. More than 430 mn people use Microsoft 365 applications, while the company reports that more than 90% of Fortune 500 businesses use Microsoft 365 Copilot. These relationships make a rapid displacement of Microsoft’s productivity suite unlikely. However, AI-native applications could eventually reduce the value customers assign to conventional software licenses or limit Microsoft’s ability to increase subscription prices. The competitive relationship is also unusual because Microsoft benefits from Anthropic’s expansion. Under an infrastructure agreement announced in November 2025, Anthropic committed to purchasing $30 bn of Azure computing capacity. Consequently, Anthropic could pressure Microsoft’s application revenue while simultaneously generating substantial demand for its cloud infrastructure. The financial outcome depends on whether Microsoft’s Azure earnings from AI developers can offset any deterioration in the pricing power or growth of its productivity software business. Claude by Anthropic+2 Microsoft is expanding beyond traditional software subscriptions through enterprise AI agents, governance tools and integrated cloud infrastructure. On November 10, Microsoft and IBM announced Imagine Enterprise, a platform designed to help organizations deploy, manage and secure AI agents in regulated industries. IBM Consulting contributes more than 6,000 prebuilt AI agents and related assets, while Microsoft supplies cloud infrastructure, AI technologies and enterprise security capabilities. The partnership targets organizations requiring extensive compliance, identity management and operational controls, including financial institutions and healthcare providers. For Microsoft, the initiative creates opportunities to generate additional Azure consumption while extending the role of Microsoft Foundry, Fabric, Copilot and Agent 365 across enterprise workflows. The investment case depends on converting experimental deployments into recurring commercial demand. Governance and security capabilities may improve Microsoft’s competitive position, particularly among organizations that cannot deploy autonomous AI systems without centralized oversight. However, the new partnership has not yet established a publicly disclosed revenue contribution sufficient to assess its effect on Microsoft’s earnings forecasts. Microsoft’s Ignite conference, scheduled for November 17 to 20, is the next major opportunity for management to address questions surrounding its AI strategy. Investment banks are looking for additional evidence of enterprise Copilot adoption, improvements in agent governance and more efficient infrastructure utilization. The conference could also provide greater visibility into how Microsoft intends to monetize autonomous AI agents across Microsoft 365, Azure and its broader enterprise platform. The most important financial indicators remain Azure capacity utilization, Microsoft 365 revenue per user, cloud gross margins and free cash flow after capital expenditures. Microsoft’s growing contractual backlog provides visibility into future sales, but investors will need to determine how quickly those commitments convert into revenue and whether infrastructure spending can produce acceptable returns. The company must also demonstrate that the latest service disruption was contained and that corrective measures can reduce the probability of similar failures. Microsoft’s next quarterly results will provide a clearer assessment of whether demand for AI computing is translating into stronger profitability, rather than simply requiring additional investment. For the stock, the distinction matters. Current valuations already incorporate sustained cloud growth and continued enterprise AI adoption. Further appreciation will depend increasingly on earnings conversion, capital efficiency and Microsoft’s ability to defend its software franchises while expanding into AI infrastructure. content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) is still struggling to restore Outlook, Teams and other workplace apps after a global outage that has lasted more than 14 hours. The disruption began on Thursday and has hit users in at least 74 countries, according to Downdetector, the outage-tracking website. On Friday morning, Microsoft said it was "seeing positive results" in improving stability and capacity, and was rolling out its fixes more widely across affected regions. Earlier, it had admitted that its repairs were not producing a sustained recovery. The company blamed "elevated load" on its infrastructure: a number of servers had become unexpectedly unavailable, leaving the remaining machines overloaded. It said it had found no sign of malicious activity and would publish the root cause once the problem was fixed. Reports of problems with Outlook peaked at about 140,000 on Thursday evening, according to Downdetector, which is more than 2,000 times the normal level. About 43,000 reports were still coming in at 7am UK time on Friday as Europe started work. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365, the company's office software suite, which includes Outlook, Teams and the Copilot AI assistant. The disruption has spread to other technology companies, with OpenAI and Anthropic both reporting problems with their own tools. Government agencies in Japan and Australia said their email systems had been affected, including Australia's domestic intelligence agency, the BBC reported. Courts in the Philippines, Singapore and North America warned that communications would be delayed. IndiGo, India's largest airline, said its email customer support was down, while its rival Air India used the moment to advertise flights on social media. The outage revives memories of July 2024, when a faulty CrowdStrike update crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers and grounded flights around the world. title: Structural Divergence in U.S. Employment Amid AI Restructuring - 富途牛牛
content: In 2026, the U.S. labor market is characterized by low layoffs and weak hiring. Microsoft and American Express are leveraging AI to optimize their workforce, and data centers are boosting the construction sector; however, entry-level white-collar positions are under pressure, real wages are declining, and risks associated with structural transformation are becoming apparent. According to Woofun AI, the U.S. labor market in fall 2026 is experiencing a profound structural divergence: despite initial jobless claims remaining at a near-57-year low of 194,000 and the overall unemployment rate standing at just 4.2%, nonfarm payrolls increased by only 29,000 jobs in September, while both hiring and separation rates have simultaneously weakened. This anomaly of "low layoffs and weak hiring" is not merely a cyclical fluctuation, but rather characterized by$Microsoft (MSFT.US)$Offering a voluntary severance package to approximately 60,000 employees,$American Express (AXP.US)$Marking a profound transformation driven by AI-powered efficiency restructuring, the company announced cuts of approximately 5% (around 3,500 employees) to its global workforce. The calmness of macro data stands in stark contrast to the aggressive micro-level behavior of firms. With about 1.7 million people continuing to claim unemployment benefits, it indicates that large-scale forced layoffs remain rare; instead, companies prefer to adjust their structures through natural attrition, such as encouraging early retirement and accepting voluntary departures without filling the vacancies. Microsoft's voluntary buyout program covers roughly a quarter of its global workforce, which is essentially a form of voluntary exit; meanwhile, American Express explicitly emphasizes preparing for AI deployment to enhance organizational agility and decision-making efficiency. According to data compiled by Woofun AI, this model of driving AI-driven efficiency restructuring through voluntary buyouts and workforce reductions is reshaping the human‑resource cost structure of tech giants, making employment relatively secure for current staff while exposing job seekers to an exceptionally challenging market environment. The polarization of the labor market has further intensified sectoral reversals. Reemployment cycles have lengthened, with those aged 20 to 24, recent graduates, and inexperienced entry-level job seekers bearing the brunt; their unemployment rates are significantly higher than the overall level. This stems from companies' cautious hiring stance: they prioritize retaining experienced staff and leverage AI tools to assign tasks previously handled by multiple junior employees to a smaller pool of highly skilled workers, thereby shrinking the number of entry-level positions. Meanwhile, the historical pattern whereby recessions are traditionally triggered by an initial contraction in interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as construction and manufacturing has shown some partial reversal. Employment in nonresidential construction has expanded markedly, driven by data-center construction, spurring a recovery in durable consumer goods manufacturing (e.g., cooling and electrical equipment). Despite a moderate contraction in residential construction, overall employment in the construction and manufacturing sectors has continued to grow net, serving as a key factor underpinning recent economic resilience, while the service sector and white-collar jobs face distinct pressures. Productivity gains have not translated into broad-based real income growth; instead, they have exacerbated distributional imbalances. Information technology, finance, and professional services are the sectors with the highest AI adoption rates. According to Census Bureau surveys, these sectors saw a pronounced upward inflection in real output per worker from late 2022 to early 2023. Together, these high-adoption industries account for roughly 15% of the workforce. Preliminary estimates suggest that about 80% to 85% of productivity gains in AI-related sectors are currently flowing to corporate profits, with only a small share passing through to real wages. As a result, nominal wages have risen by around 3.0% year over year, while the consumer price index has increased by approximately 3.7%, leading to a modest decline in real wages. Workers, long accustomed to real wage growth of about 2% to 2.5%, are feeling greater strain from major expenses such as housing and automobiles, and the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index has remained persistently low. In this self-reinforcing cycle, firms reinvest excess profits into AI infrastructure, while small businesses—accounting for more than 40 percent of employment and GDP—face heightened uncertainty. According to an NFIB survey, in September 2026 their optimism index was slightly below its long-term average, while the uncertainty index stood well above historical norms; concerns about labor quality, inflation, volatile tariff policies, and energy price shocks have made them cautious in hiring plans. In the outlook ahead, Federal Reserve policy remains a key variable. Current leading indicators have improved across the board, except for residential construction, and corporate profits remain resilient, giving the economy some capacity to absorb further rate hikes. However, if policy continues to tighten and this translates into a marked weakening of employment in construction and manufacturing, cyclical pressures could compound and exacerbate existing structural frictions. The sustained moderate decline in residential construction employment warrants close monitoring, as it has historically foreshadowed recessions. Real wage growth is unlikely to improve significantly by 2027; deep-seated structural factors—such as the negative externalities stemming from excessive government debt and spending—continue to restrain real income growth in the private sector. The market is currently in a transitional phase: blue-collar jobs are supported by data-center construction, while entry-level white-collar positions face pressure. Policy responses should prioritize lowering barriers to retraining and improving mechanisms for creating entry-level opportunities, thereby preventing an expansion of the public sector from imposing prolonged downward pressure on private-sector real incomes. The definition of "labor-market security" is being redefined, shifting from mere unemployment status to the ability to sustainably accumulate experience and achieve real income growth amid a rapidly evolving technological landscape. title: Microsoft apologizes for massive outage that took down Outlook and other 365 services - CNBC
content:
Microsoft issued an apology Friday for a wide-ranging outage that shut down Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products, as the company worked to restore service nearly 24 hours after connectivity problems began. “We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” a Microsoft spokesperson said Friday. “We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.” In a statement, Microsoft said the connectivity disruption stemmed from “an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade.” The software giant said the underlying cause of the outage had been addressed and that they were still working to restore services to some customers. Engineers scrambled to solve connectivity problems that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday. Email and calendar service Outlook, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, were largely down during the morning hours in the U.S. on Friday and throughout the Asian and European business days. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products were also hit. Users began to regain access to email and other services Friday morning. In an update around 10:30 a.m. ET, Microsoft noted “encouraging recovery progress” and said that “service availability and email delivery performance [was] improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure” as Outlook and other Microsoft 365 tools began to come back online. In an earlier update Friday morning, Microsoft said that email queues were “approaching normal levels,” but that intermittent issues were expected as recovery efforts continue. It had previously given updates by region, with Asia Pacific services among the first to start normalizing. Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online gradually stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages. Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. The company said it would issue a full report once its assessment of the outage was complete. The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure “elevated load across multiple regions,” caused by a “number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure.” Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said. Governments and businesses across the U.S., Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption. The U.K.’s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls “may be subject to long waits” as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X. Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage. U.S. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told CNBC’s “The Exchange” that he asked for a briefing on the outage. Gottheimer worked at Microsoft prior to serving in Congress. “Is there something that went on that’s nefarious here, or is this just something else? These outages occur in a lot of the companies, but the size of it and the length of it and the timing of it,” Gottheimer said. Air India said it had “temporarily rerouted” emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected. Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft “believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Reuters reported. A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world’s biggest IT system outages in 2024, hitting airlines, banks and more. Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users. The incident highlights a business “resilience and dependency issue that has been decades in the making,” James Owen, managing partner of Digital Risks at consultancy Control Risks, said by phone. “We have become, organizationally in the private sector and more broadly, increasingly dependent on a smaller segment of technology and infrastructure as critical to daily life and business activities.” “Organizations are becoming more aware through a geopolitical lens about what technologies they adopt, whether their services are provided by firms in the U.S., or China, or elsewhere, but this shows the importance of proper recovery planning in the case of an IT outage. That could be manual backups, protocols that do not require internet connection, investing in diverse suppliers and crisis management planning rehearsals,” he said. Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday. Amazon wrote on X that services were “operating normally” and an “unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports.” The company referred users to its health dashboard for “accurate data.” At 4 p.m. ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had “validated an alternative service health check method” that brought some affected servers back online. “We’re now applying this change more broadly,” Microsoft wrote. “We’re also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses.” Got a confidential news tip? title: MSFT Stock Reverses and Heads to $500 After Microsoft 365 Services Impacted by Outlook Outage - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft shares retreat toward $520 after a service disruption affects Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Microsoft 365, adding another source of uncertainty as investors reassess rising infrastructure costs, competition from Anthropic and the profitability of cloud expansion. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have extended their retreat from record highs near $560, falling toward $520 as investors confront another setback for the technology giant. The stock had recovered sharply from the $500 area following the U.S. midterm elections, but renewed concerns about infrastructure spending, competition and operational reliability have weakened sentiment. Thursday’s decline accelerated after disruptions affected several Microsoft services, including Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Microsoft 365. Users reported difficulties accessing email, workplace collaboration tools and other cloud-based applications, while Microsoft warned that the disruption could affect service connectivity across multiple regions. Downdetector recorded more than 130,000 reports of Outlook problems at 1:27 p.m. ET, alongside more than 46,000 reports involving Microsoft 365 and approximately 3,000 concerning Teams. These figures represent user-submitted reports rather than confirmed numbers of affected customers. Microsoft initially said it had resolved a Teams disruption affecting North American users, but subsequently indicated that the wider connectivity issue could affect Microsoft 365 customers internationally. Although temporary service disruptions do not necessarily indicate a structural problem, the incident highlights the dependence of businesses on Microsoft’s cloud-based productivity ecosystem. The outage comes as Microsoft faces growing scrutiny over the cost and scale of its infrastructure expansion. Noelle Walsh, President of Cloud Operations and Innovation, reiterated that Microsoft would finance its own data-centre construction and associated infrastructure. Her comments extend a community-first commitment announced in January 2026, under which the company pledged to cover electricity costs and grid upgrades associated with its projects rather than transferring those expenses to local residents. Walsh oversees Microsoft’s global data-centre operations, managing approximately 15,000 employees and a multibillion-dollar investment programme. While covering infrastructure costs could reduce community opposition and regulatory friction, it also reinforces the financial burden associated with expanding Azure and computing capacity. Investors increasingly want evidence that additional infrastructure can generate sufficient revenue without weakening margins and free cash flow. Competition is another emerging concern after Anthropic introduced workplace software targeting markets dominated by Microsoft and Google. Its products include a videoconferencing assistant, data dashboards and Claude Sheets, a spreadsheet service positioned against Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets. The company also plans to allow enterprises to integrate existing applications into Claude, potentially turning the platform into a central interface for workplace activities. This represents a competitive challenge for Microsoft’s productivity ecosystem. Microsoft 365 Cloud generated $27.78 billion in first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue, ended September 30, 2026, increasing approximately 17% year-over-year and accounting for around 30% of total company revenue. Although this includes broader commercial and consumer cloud services, it demonstrates the importance of the productivity business to Microsoft’s financial performance. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months which has now turned into a support zone, and climbed above $550 earlier in October but slipped toward $500 again on Monday. The price slip breached the 50 daily SMA in September which has been acting as support and we’re seeing a rebound today. The price has now pushed to a new record high above $555 area which represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MSFT buyers gave up at this zone, reversing lower below $520 today. Microsoft’s latest quarterly results remained impressive. Net income increased 32% year-over-year to $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, while revenue climbed to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year-over-year, or 31% in constant currency. However, strong earnings have not eliminated concerns about the capital required to maintain growth. Data centres, servers, networking equipment and specialised processors require substantial upfront investment, and investors increasingly want measurable returns rather than larger spending commitments. An amended filing concerning Microsoft’s relationship with Anthropic identifies at least $44.9 billion in commitments through June 2033, subject to contractual delivery and breach provisions. Microsoft is also developing its Maia 300 custom processor, reportedly targeting 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems. Its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to improve rack-scale computing capacity. Custom silicon could eventually reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers, but development and deployment require additional investment before those efficiency gains translate into stronger profitability. Microsoft’s latest retreat reflects several overlapping concerns: service reliability, rising infrastructure costs, Anthropic’s competitive expansion and questions about future returns. The company’s strong earnings and cloud growth remain important positives, but investors are becoming increasingly selective about the financial benefits of expanding computing capacity. With MSFT retreating from $560 toward $520, the immediate technical focus shifts to whether buyers can defend the $520 area. A sustained recovery will require renewed buying interest and stronger confidence that Microsoft’s infrastructure investments can deliver profitable growth without undermining free cash flow.

title: Morgan Stanley previews next week's Microsoft (MSFT.US) Ignite conference: The "enterprise AI flywheel" faces a critical test, with five key focal points. - 富途牛牛
content: Microsoft's Ignite conference opens next week, and Morgan Stanley treats it as a review rather than a launch event. The Zhitong Finance APP has learned that Microsoft (MSFT.US)'s Ignite conference opens next week, and Morgan Stanley views it as a validation event rather than a launch event. In a forward-looking report released on Thursday, the firm maintained an "Overweight" rating and a $650 price target. The report's focus is not on new products, but on whether a closed loop can be proven to have been established: Azure provides computing power, Fabric offers an enterprise context, Foundry orchestrates models and agents, and M365 together with Copilot integrates intelligence into employees' daily workflows. Morgan Stanley refers to these four layers as the "Enterprise AI Flywheel" and believes Ignite's value lies in demonstrating that it is translating into broader production deployments and higher full-stack consumption. The conference will be held in San Francisco from November 17 to 20. The core session is scheduled for 1 p.m. EST on November 17 (2 a.m. Beijing time on November 18), followed by a sell-side Q&A with CEO Satya Nadella at 4 p.m.; on November 18 at 3 p.m., Morgan Stanley will meet with CFO Amy Hood and Vice President of Investor Relations Jonathan Neilson. The foundation is solid, but we need to clearly explain what makes it so. The report is based on the first fiscal quarter of 2027, released on October 28. Revenue for the quarter reached $92.3 billion, up 19% year over year; Azure grew 48% (at constant currency, accelerating 6 percentage points sequentially), and M365 commercial cloud accelerated to 18% (at constant currency). Operating margin was approximately 50%. According to Morgan Stanley, this mix supports its view of revenue growth "remaining in the high teens and accelerating toward the low 20s," as well as profit growth above 20%. However, Azure's 48% growth rate warrants a closer look: both the enterprise and small-to-medium business segments are strengthening simultaneously, driven by core cloud services and AI infrastructure together—not by any single customer type. Commercial remaining performance obligations (RPO) reached $677 billion, up 73% year over year, with roughly 30% expected to convert within the next 12 months. This provides strong revenue visibility and underpins management's confidence to continue increasing capital expenditures. Morgan Stanley has identified five key observations for this conference, which essentially represent a deconstruction of its "flywheel": First, Copilot's next frontier is ARPU, not seat count. The report's three-pillar thesis is: direct seat penetration, migration to E7 plans, and usage-based billing. The significance of the third pillar is that it can expand Microsoft's revenue boundaries from "software budgets" to "budgets for knowledge work and business processes." The two figures cited in the report are: Copilot's daily active users increased by approximately 50% quarter-over-quarter, and customers actively consuming credits increased by over 75% quarter-over-quarter. Second, Foundry's value has shifted from "providing you with models" to "managing how you use the models." In the first fiscal quarter, Foundry revenue more than tripled year over year, and the number of customers building multi-model agentic solutions increased fivefold year over year. Based on this, Morgan Stanley believes that greater model diversity is a boon rather than a burden for Microsoft—because the more customers switch among multiple models, the more they need a unified orchestration layer. Third, Fabric operates within an "enterprise context." As the underlying model itself becomes a commodity, governed enterprise data and context become the sources of differentiation. In the first fiscal quarter, more than 19,000 customers used both Fabric and Foundry, up from just over 17,000 last quarter. While the growth rate isn't rapid, it signals that customers are willing to bring their data onto the platform. Fourth, the widespread adoption of proxies is turning security into an entry point. As proxies begin accessing corporate data and performing actions across applications, customers must manage their identities, permissions, and behaviors. Consequently, the relevance of Entra, Defender, and Purview increases, further justifying the upgrade path from M365 to E5/E7. Agent 365, unveiled at Ignite last year, marks the starting point of this trajectory. Fifth, the Maia 300 is a variable on the cost curve. As long as demand continues to exceed supply, the deployment roadmap for in-house chips, the workloads they support, and their cost advantage relative to third-party solutions will be key to determining whether Azure's product‑level gross margin can improve. Gross margins are trending lower, but that's not the whole story. Improvements at the Azure product level partially offset the structural pressure from the rising share of Azure revenue; more importantly, the additional capacity freed up through efficiency gains was allocated to Foundry and quickly monetized—thereby supporting both revenue growth and operating leverage. According to Morgan Stanley's model, the trajectory of this curve is clear: gross margin declines from 67.9% in fiscal year 2026 to 65.9% in fiscal year 2027, 64.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 63.5% in fiscal year 2029, while operating margin remains virtually unchanged—46.8%, 46.6%, 46.7%, and 47.2%. In other words, the erosion in gross margin is offset by operating leverage—this is the key to whether this round of AI-related spending can be tolerated: the market will accept a decline in gross margin only if operating margin holds steady. The $650 base-case scenario corresponds to about 26 times FY2028 EPS of $24.41. On a reported basis, 26 times is a slight premium to large-cap software peers, and a 1.2x PEG ratio is below Microsoft's historical level and that of its peers. In the bull case, at $800, this implies roughly 29 times, or $27.41; in the bear case, at $300, it implies $22.25. The probabilities derived from implied volatility of options are: approximately 23.0% of reaching above $650, about 6.1% of reaching above $800, and roughly 6.8% of falling below $300. There is virtually no disagreement in the sell-side consensus: 97% overweight, 3% neutral, and 0% underweight. This forward-looking blind spot happens to be the one the market cares about most this week: Microsoft has stopped disclosing the number of paid Copilot seats. For the three consecutive quarters prior, paid seats (which last exceeded 30 million in disclosures) were the most direct metric for outsiders to gauge the progress of its AI implementation. However, this figure disappeared from the first fiscal quarter's earnings press release and conference call. Chief Financial Officer Hood told analysts that "no update on Copilot numbers was disclosed" this quarter, instead pointing to "momentum in revenue and usage." Nadella cited a "nearly 50% quarter-over-quarter increase" in daily active users and a "more than 75% quarter-over-quarter increase" in customers consuming credits, neither of which provided any baseline figures. This coincides with Microsoft's shift in pricing. The $99 M365 E7 suite and Agent 365 have already pushed customers toward a hybrid "seat fee + metered" model; Copilot Business, sold through the cloud solution provider channel, defaults to usage-based billing for new purchases and imposes a cap of 4,000 Copilot Credits per user per month—arrangements originally scheduled to take effect on December 1 were postponed to January–March 2027 following partner feedback. Morgan Stanley cites "50% increase in daily active users" as evidence of demand, but without access to the underlying seat numbers, the true significance of these percentages hinges on what their denominators actually represent. Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, told the media that many organizations are "still trying to figure out exactly what this Copilot is useful for"—whether it serves as "a fancy search tool" or as an agent integrated into workflows. This very question is precisely what Ignite must address—and Morgan Stanley assumes it already has. Two conditions that must both be true simultaneously The report's logic hinges on two conditions being met simultaneously: revenue must keep pace with rising consumption after Copilot switches to a pay-as-you-go model, and capital expenditure intensity must stop increasing. Capital spending in the first fiscal quarter was $45.2 billion (including finance leases), while the company guides for over $50 billion in the second fiscal quarter and approximately $170 billion for the full fiscal year 2027; free cash flow stood at $18.6 billion, down 27% year over year, making it the only one of the three major cloud providers still posting positive free cash flow. So at Ignite, what's truly worth listening to isn't how many agent templates were announced, but three key questions: how Copilot will be priced on a metered basis; whether Foundry can maintain its position in the orchestration layer within a multi‑model world; and whether its in‑house chips can drive down the cost per unit of compute. The first two determine the revenue ceiling, while the third sets the profit floor. In another report, Citi set a price target of $680 and assigned a "buy" rating, with reasoning similar to this report: Following a strong first fiscal quarter, Azure has reached an inflection point, and the conference will focus on infrastructure, proprietary cutting-edge models, Foundry, and the Copilot+IQ strategy. If the market turns, how far has Microsoft stock fallen before, and how long did the shares take to come back? At its worst, Microsoft stock fell 58% during the 2008-2009 Global Financial Crisis, compared with a 53% drop for the S&P 500. This marked the stock’s deepest fall in the market shocks since 2007. Across all 15 of those shocks, the stock fell 17.4% on average, slightly more than the 15.8% average for the S&P 500. Recovery has usually taken a few months, though not every time. The median wait from the low back to the old high was 2.6 months. After the 2010 Eurozone Sovereign Debt Crisis, the shares needed 19.1 months to recover. Following the 2008-2009 crisis, the wait stretched to 49.7 months. Microsoft’s Profits Still Cover Its Data Center Spending Microsoft’s profit has kept growing, although less cash is left over than a year ago. Over the twelve months to September 30, 2026, Microsoft’s revenue was $346 billion, up 17.9% from a year earlier. The company’s operating margin rose to 47.1% in the twelve months to September 2026, up from 46.3% in the twelve months to September 2025. Free cash flow, the cash left after spending on data centers and equipment, fell to $60.0 billion over the same twelve months, down from $78.0 billion a year earlier. content: Microsoft stock retreat from the record high near $560 as renewed data-centre spending commitments, competition from Anthropic’s workplace software and questions about future infrastructure returns weigh on investor sentiment. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have reversed their recent rally, falling more than 2.5% toward $520 after approaching $560 last week. The decline follows a strong recovery from the $500 area, supported by improving sentiment across technology stocks after the U.S. midterm elections. However, enthusiasm is fading as investors reassess the costs of expanding cloud infrastructure and the returns expected from massive computing commitments. Fresh pressure emerged after Noelle Walsh, Microsoft’s President of Cloud Operations and Innovation, reiterated that the company would pay for its own data-centre construction and associated infrastructure. The commitment comes as communities increasingly question who should cover the electricity networks, power lines, substations and utility upgrades required by large data-centre developments. Walsh oversees Microsoft’s global data-centre operations, managing approximately 15,000 employees and a multibillion-dollar investment programme. Her comments extend a community-first commitment announced in January 2026, under which Microsoft pledged to cover electricity costs and grid infrastructure upgrades associated with its projects rather than passing those expenses on to local residents. The company operates hundreds of facilities supporting Azure and its expanding computing workloads. Although taking responsibility for infrastructure costs could help reduce community opposition and regulatory friction, it also reinforces the financial burden associated with Microsoft’s expansion strategy. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the revenue generated by additional computing capacity will justify the substantial investment required to build and operate these facilities. Competition is another emerging concern after Anthropic introduced a new suite of workplace software targeting markets dominated by Microsoft and Google. The products include a videoconferencing assistant, data dashboards and Claude Sheets, a spreadsheet service positioned against Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets. Several tools are reportedly available in beta to paying customers. More importantly, Anthropic plans to allow enterprises to integrate existing applications into Claude, potentially positioning its platform as a central interface for workplace activities rather than simply an assistant operating alongside traditional software. This creates a competitive challenge for Microsoft’s productivity ecosystem. Microsoft 365 Cloud generated $27.78 billion in revenue during the first quarter of fiscal 2027, ended September 30, 2026, representing approximately 17% year-over-year growth and around 30% of total company revenue. While this figure covers the broader productivity cloud business rather than Excel alone, it illustrates the importance of the segment to Microsoft’s financial performance. Microsoft’s latest quarterly results remained impressive. Net income increased 32% year-over-year to $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue climbed to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, comfortably exceeding expectations, while earnings surpassed the analyst consensus of $4.27 per share. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year-over-year, or 31% in constant currency. CEO Satya Nadella highlighted improvements in computing capacity, customer choice, security and cost efficiency. Nevertheless, strong earnings have not removed concerns about capital expenditure, particularly as data centres, servers, networking equipment and specialised processors require enormous upfront investment. Investors increasingly want evidence that cloud growth can translate into sustainable profitability without weakening margins and free cash flow. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months which has now turned into a support zone, and climbed above $550 earlier in October but slipped toward $500 again on Monday. The price slip breached the 50 daily SMA in September which has been acting as support and we’re seeing a rebound today. The price has now pushed to a new record high above $555 area which represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MSFT buyers gave up at this zone, reversing lower below $520 today. An amended filing concerning Microsoft’s relationship with Anthropic identifies at least $44.9 billion in commitments through June 2033, subject to contractual delivery and breach provisions. While the arrangement highlights substantial future computing demand, it also raises questions about the financial obligations required to support expanding infrastructure capacity. Microsoft is attempting to improve those economics through its own silicon development. Its Maia 300 processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver significantly higher rack-scale throughput than Maia 200. Custom processors could eventually reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers. However, development and deployment require additional investment before those efficiency improvements translate into stronger returns. Microsoft’s consumer businesses offer a less encouraging picture. The Devices and Consumer segment generated $15.5 billion in revenue, down 3% year-over-year. Search and advertising revenue increased 12%, but Xbox content and services declined 2%, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue dropped 22%. Regulatory pressure is another consideration. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority has proposed designating Microsoft as having strategic market status in certain software markets, potentially increasing scrutiny of licensing, pricing and product bundling. For MSFT investors, the challenge is becoming increasingly clear: Microsoft continues to deliver strong revenue and earnings growth, but the cost of maintaining its competitive position is rising. With shares retreating from $560 toward $520, investors may demand stronger evidence that infrastructure expansion and future computing commitments can generate sufficient returns to justify current valuations.

title: Anthropic Now Makes Its Own Spreadsheet Software. Here's What I'd Do With Microsoft Stock. - The Motley Fool
content: Claude Sheets is still in beta. Should the Excel maker's shareholders worry? Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) firm behind the Claude chatbot, now has a spreadsheet of its own. On Tuesday, Nov. 10, it released Claude Sheets and Claude Whiteboards in beta, and made its dashboard tool generally available under a new name, Claude Data. This gives Claude an alternative to Excel. Microsoft (MSFT +0.17%) sells Excel as part of Microsoft 365, a business that pulled in about $111 billion in revenue for the software giant's fiscal 2026, which ended June 30. Microsoft shares dropped 2.2% on Tuesday, to roughly $533, but they're still up about 10% this year as I write. I don't think a beta spreadsheet is a reason to sell the stock. But the launch is a good excuse to look at the business it overlaps with -- and one number in it that's been cooling. According to Anthropic's launch post, Claude Sheets can make a spreadsheet with tabs, formulas, formatting, and drop-down menus, often from one prompt. Claude changes the cells directly, and colleagues can work on the same sheet together. Anthropic is open about the limits, though. Its post says the sheets have "simple spreadsheet functionality" for now. And for anyone who needs everything Excel can do, it suggests exporting the file to .xlsx or CSV, or using Claude for Excel, which works in Microsoft's own spreadsheet. The rollout to big companies is cautious, too. Sheets and Whiteboards are on by default for Team plans but off by default for Enterprise customers. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. That might change as Anthropic adds features. But companies typically get Excel as part of Microsoft 365, a subscription that also includes email, Teams, file storage, and security tools. A better spreadsheet alone wouldn't replace all of that. Microsoft 365's commercial and consumer businesses brought in around a third of the $332 billion of revenue Microsoft reported for fiscal 2026. Profit's tougher to nail down, because Microsoft now reports Microsoft 365 in a new agents and infra segment that also covers Azure, its cloud computing platform. Under the old setup, though, the productivity and business processes segment (Microsoft 365 plus LinkedIn and Dynamics) made $83.9 billion in operating income in fiscal 2026, up 20% from a year earlier. This was around 54% of the company's total, making it Microsoft's most profitable segment by a big margin. And the business keeps growing fast. In the fiscal first quarter of 2027 (from July through September 2026), Microsoft 365 cloud revenue rose 17% year over year to $27.8 billion, or around 30% of total revenue. Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue also grew 17%, near the 16% to 20% pace it kept through fiscal 2026. Plus, management sees around 19% growth in constant currency (leaving out exchange-rate moves) this quarter, with growth picking up through the year. The number to watch is seats. Growth in paid Microsoft 365 commercial seats was 6% to 7% year over year in each of the four quarters of fiscal 2026. In the fiscal first quarter, it slowed to 5%. In other words, more of Microsoft's growth is coming from charging each user more. Revenue per user climbed on upgrades to premium plans, such as Microsoft 365 Copilot (its AI assistant for work) and the E5 and E7 bundles. CFO Amy Hood linked some of the seat slowdown to "weaker sales execution" in Microsoft's standard E3 plan and stand-alone products on the Oct. 28 earnings call. Notably, the quarter closed weeks before Claude Sheets arrived, so the release wasn't behind it. Still, if a rival tool starts winning over Microsoft's customers, seat growth is likely where it'd turn up first. Microsoft reported $18.04 per share over the past four quarters on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis, excluding gains and losses from its OpenAI stake. At roughly $533, that's about 30 times adjusted earnings. Adjusted earnings per share climbed 18% year over year last quarter, so this isn't an excessively high price. But it doesn't leave much room for seat growth to keep sliding. For investors who already hold Microsoft, I don't see a reason to sell over a spreadsheet that steers its heaviest users back to Excel. For new money, though, I think the stock's a little too pricey here.
